chapters.title: First, Get the Name Right — And the Problem It Solved
chapters.intro: First, the correction everyone needs: this is Tower Bridge, not London Bridge — that plainer crossing is half a mile upstream. Second surprise: it opened in 1894, a contemporary of the Eiffel Tower. Under the medieval-looking stone is a Victorian steel machine, built because the East End had outgrown every other crossing.

subchapters.title: London Bridge Versus Tower Bridge
subchapters.text: Look upstream and you can see the real London Bridge: a functional, low, modern concrete crossing with a famous name and a long history — Roman, medieval and Georgian bridges all stood near that site, and the medieval one carried houses and shops for 600 years. This Gothic fairytale beside the Tower is Tower Bridge, opened 30 June 1894 by the Prince of Wales, the future Edward VII. Tourists have confused the two for a century — an American buyer in 1968 famously purchased the previous London Bridge for Arizona amid a persistent, denied rumour that he thought he was buying this one. The tea towels are not helping, but now you know: name, date and function are all different.

subchapters.title: The East End Problem — Docks, People and a Jammed River
subchapters.text: By the 1870s London's East End had exploded with docks, warehouses and housing, and workers east of London Bridge had no nearby crossing — the Tower Subway tunnel and ferries could not cope, and a detour to London Bridge could add hours to a cart's day. But any new low bridge would block tall-masted ships from the Pool of London, the busy port immediately upstream, then the greatest concentration of shipping in the world. Parliament therefore demanded a crossing that served road and river at once. A special committee considered the problem from 1876, and over 50 designs were submitted — swing bridges, transporter bridges, even a design with a huge rotating platform and one with steep spiral approaches for carts.

subchapters.title: Why a Bascule — The Seesaw Solution
subchapters.text: The chosen answer was a bascule bridge — bascule is French for seesaw. The central roadway splits into two leaves, each pivoting on a shaft in the base of a tower, with a massive counterweight at its short rear end balancing the long span that reaches across the river. Raise them, and a ship passes through a clear opening 61 metres wide with 41 metres of headroom, as Parliament specified. Lower them, and road traffic flows. The genius is the counterweight: the machinery does not lift 1,000 tons of steel from dead weight; it tips a balanced seesaw, so a modest engine, given stored hydraulic power, could raise each leaf to 83 degrees in about a minute. Everything else in this exhibition is commentary on that one elegant idea.

subchapters.title: Horace Jones and John Wolfe Barry
subchapters.text: The bridge had two fathers. Sir Horace Jones, architect and surveyor to the City of London, promoted the bascule idea and gave the bridge its form — and, awkwardly, sat among the judges of the competition his own design effectively won, a very Victorian arrangement. Sir John Wolfe Barry, son of the architect Charles Barry who designed the Palace of Westminster, engineered it: towers on piers, suspension side spans, hydraulic machinery. Jones died in 1887, a year after work began; Barry completed the bridge with Jones's assistant George D. Stevenson, who redesigned the stone facing in the form you see today. When you admire the bridge, you are looking at an architect's silhouette filled with an engineer's skeleton.

chapters.caption: Tower Bridge from the south bank — steel frame dressed in Cornish granite and Portland stone

chapters.title: A Machine Dressed as a Castle — Steel, Stone and Gothic Dress
chapters.intro: Parliament required the bridge to be built in Gothic style to harmonise with the Tower of London next door. So 11,000 tons of steel were clothed in Cornish granite and Portland stone, with carved detail, mock battlements and tall slate roofs. Look closely: every 'medieval' feature is doing a modern structural job, or hiding one.

subchapters.title: 11,000 Tons of Steel Under the Stone
subchapters.text: The towers and walkways are a steel frame built by Sir William Arrol and Company of Glasgow — the firm that had just built the Forth Bridge in Scotland. More than 11,000 tons of steel went into the frame, erected first and then clad, so the stone you touch is a weatherproof skin, not the structure. This mattered for speed and strength: steel could carry the suspension chains of the side spans and the enormous pivot loads of the bascules, which no masonry tower of this slenderness could have borne. Riveters worked in teams high over the river, heating rivets in braziers and driving them home — the bridge is held together by hundreds of thousands of them, each hammered in by hand.

subchapters.title: Cornish Granite and Portland Stone — The Chosen Costume
subchapters.text: George Stevenson, completing Jones's work, changed the intended brick facing to stone: Cornish granite for the hard-wearing lower work and plinths, pale Portland stone — the stone of St Paul's Cathedral and the Tower's own White Tower — for the towers above. The choice tied the new bridge visually to London's two most famous stone buildings. Look for the carved coats of arms, the traceried windows and the steep roofs with their gilded finials. None of it is structural, and the Victorians knew it; the Gothic dress was a planning condition and a public-relations triumph — Londoners accepted a radical machine because it arrived dressed as a castle gateway.

subchapters.title: The Suspension Side Spans — Chains Over Your Head
subchapters.text: Between each tower and its bank, the roadway hangs from suspension chains — look up as you cross at street level and you will see the great steel chains sweeping from the tower tops down to anchorages in the abutments. The high-level walkways are not just footbridges: they contain tie rods that resist the outward pull of those chains, tying the two towers together against the tension of the side spans. That is why the walkways had to be built before the bridge could fully work as designed, and why they are so massively framed. The bridge is thus two bridges in one: a suspension bridge on each side, a seesaw in the middle, sharing the same pair of towers.

subchapters.title: The Colour Scheme — Red, White and Blue Since 1977
subchapters.text: The bridge's familiar colours are not Victorian. For most of its life the steelwork was painted in practical browns and chocolates — a colour sometimes called Tower Bridge brown — to resist soot and rust. The present red, white and blue scheme dates from 1977, when the bridge was repainted for Queen Elizabeth II's Silver Jubilee, and it proved so popular it was kept through later restorations. The stonework, cleaned in the 2000s restoration after a century of London grime, returned to a pale honey colour that startles people who grew up with the sooty version. Repainting the whole structure takes years and is done in sections, from pontoons and scaffolds, without closing the bridge to traffic for more than brief periods.

subchapters.title: Grade I Listed and Still Working — A Listed Machine
subchapters.text: Tower Bridge is Grade I listed — the highest category of protection — yet unlike most listed structures it must move, daily, under load. That dual identity drives its engineering culture: original fabric is preserved wherever possible, the Victorian engines are maintained as museum pieces in working order, and modern machinery is fitted reversibly where it can be. Even the bascules' timber-block road surface was replaced thoughtfully — the original deck was paved with wood blocks, quieter under iron-shod horses and cart wheels, some of which survive in the exhibition. As you go up the North Tower, keep asking of everything you see: is that 1894, or a careful replacement? The exhibition is honest about the answers.
subchapters.directions: Enter the Exhibition in the North Tower, on the Tower of London side, and take the lift or the 206 steps up.

chapters.caption: Steel frame, stone skin — the towers from the river

chapters.title: Building It, 1886–1894 — Piers, Caissons and Divers
chapters.intro: Construction took eight years, five major contractors and about 432 workers, and cost £1,184,000. Two massive piers containing over 70,000 tons of concrete were sunk into the riverbed. The exhibition in the towers tells the builders' story with photographs, tools and one very heavy diving suit — stand beside it before you judge Victorian engineering as abstract.

subchapters.title: Sinking the Piers — Working Inside Iron Boxes
subchapters.text: The towers stand not on the riverbed but on piers sunk through it. Sir John Jackson's men worked inside caissons — huge iron boxes lowered to the river bottom — digging out clay from within while the box sank under its own weight, in compressed air that kept the Thames out. Compressed-air work was dangerous and poorly understood: men suffered joint pains and, in severe cases, the bends, as decompression sickness came to be called, and shifts were strictly timed. Once the caissons reached firm ground they were filled with concrete — over 70,000 tons across both piers — creating artificial islands of foundation in the middle of a working river, while shipping passed on either side throughout.

subchapters.title: The Divers in Brass Helmets
subchapters.text: Look for the standard diving dress on display: a copper-and-brass helmet, a weighted canvas suit, lead-soled boots and an air line to a hand pump on a boat above. Divers in this kit worked on the riverbed in near darkness, by touch, checking caissons, placing concrete and clearing obstructions in water so murky that vision was measured in inches. The whole suit weighs around 80 kilos; a diver could barely walk on deck and was helpless if his air line fouled. Standing next to it makes the statistics of this bridge physical: behind every clean line in the architect's drawing was a man kneeling in cold mud at the bottom of the Thames, breathing through a tube.

subchapters.title: 432 Workers, Ten Deaths — The Human Ledger
subchapters.text: About 432 construction workers built the bridge over eight years. The records count 29 serious injuries and 10 deaths — falls from height, drowning, crushing — at a time of no harnesses, no safety netting and piece-rate pressure to work fast. The exhibition names and photographs ordinary workmen — riveters, stonemasons, labourers perched on beams in flat caps — an unusually democratic touch for a Victorian monument, which usually remembered only its architect. Take the stairs in the North Tower if your knees allow: the stairwells double as exhibition space precisely so that you climb through the builders' story at the pace they climbed, rather than arriving by lift having skipped it.

subchapters.title: Five Contractors, One Bridge — Who Built What
subchapters.text: The work was divided among specialists: Sir John Jackson built the foundations; William Webster built much of the masonry and approaches; Sir William Arrol and Company erected the steelwork; Armstrong Mitchell of Newcastle — Baron Armstrong's firm — supplied the hydraulic machinery; and Sir H. H. Bartlett was among the principal building contractors. Coordinating five firms, river traffic, tides and London's weather for eight years was itself an engineering achievement, run from site offices on the piers. The bridge opened on 30 June 1894 — on time enough, over budget as Barry ruefully recorded, and immediately successful: over 8,000 pedestrians crossed on opening day by some counts, and the bascules began their working life that has never since stopped.

subchapters.title: The Rejected Designs — The Bridge London Didn't Get
subchapters.text: Before you leave the tower displays, look for the rejected competition designs. London could have had Joseph Bazalgette's elegant high-level bridge — rejected for insufficient headroom for ships — or a low swing bridge that would have blocked the road for long periods, or designs with lifts, ramps and rotating platforms that look like fairground rides. Horace Jones himself had earlier proposed a very different scheme. Exhibiting the losers is more than filler: it shows how open the question was, and how contingent the icon is. The most recognisable bridge in the world exists in this form because a committee in 1884 preferred a seesaw in Gothic dress to every alternative Victorian ingenuity could draw.
subchapters.directions: Ride the lift — or climb the stairs — to the top of the North Tower for the walkways.

chapters.caption: Inside the North Tower — construction photos, divers' suits and the builders' stories

chapters.title: The North Tower — Lift, Stairs and the View That Opens
chapters.intro: Whether you ride or climb, the North Tower is the exhibition's front door and its archive: films, portraits, the bridge's control story and the first reveal of height. At the top, doors open onto the walkways 42 metres above the river — and London rearranges itself around you.

subchapters.title: 206 Steps and the Stairwell Exhibition
subchapters.text: The North Tower contains 206 steps to walkway level, and the climb is curated: landings carry photographs of construction, portraits of the bridge's engineers and masters, and panels on the river's history. Notice the tower's interior structure as you climb — you are inside a steel frame, and in places the exhibition leaves girders and rivets exposed rather than panelled over, so the building explains itself. The original towers had steam lifts for pedestrians using the walkways; today's electric lifts serve the exhibition, and step-free access runs through both towers. If you took the lift, double back to at least one stair landing: the divers' and builders' material is the soul of this floor.

subchapters.title: The Bridge Master and the Control Room Story
subchapters.text: A bridge that lifts on demand needs a commander. The Bridge Master and the bridge's team — today a small crew, once a staff of about 80 including engine-room crews, lift operators and toll and gate staff — coordinate every lift with river traffic, the Port of London Authority and road traffic control. Ships must give 24 hours' notice; lifts are scheduled, published and run to the minute, because a lift stops a major road. Displays in the tower show the modern control panels alongside the Victorian speaking tubes and signal systems they replaced. The bridge has right-of-way rules worthy of a railway: river traffic takes precedence over road traffic, a legal priority that survives from 1894 and that no mayor or motorist can override.

subchapters.title: The Towers as Homes and Offices
subchapters.text: The towers were never only machinery and stairs. They contained offices for the Bridge Master and his staff, stores, workshops and, in the bridge's early decades, accommodation connected with the operating crew — a small vertical workplace above the river. Traces remain in the domestic-scale windows, fireplaces and room divisions you pass on the exhibition route, which sit oddly, and charmingly, inside a structure most people read as solid stone. The bridge was also a workplace with weather: tower staff logged fog, ice and flood, and during the great smogs of the 1950s the towers stood above a river on which navigation had effectively stopped, the walkways in cloud while the bascules waited for ships that could not move.

subchapters.title: Films and the View from the Tower Windows
subchapters.text: At walkway level, short films compress the bridge's life: a lift filmed from the bascule chamber, time-lapse of a day's traffic, archive footage of the opening. Watch one before you step out — it calibrates your eye. Then look from the tower windows themselves, before the walkway: downstream, the Thames bends past Wapping and Rotherhithe toward Canary Wharf; upstream, the Tower of London sits at eye level in a way it never does from the ground. You are 42 metres up — 138 feet — roughly the height of a 14-storey building, but crucially you are mid-river, a vantage no skyscraper offers, because every other viewpoint in London stands on a bank looking across, not on the water looking along.

chapters.caption: From the North Tower — the river opens in both directions

chapters.title: How a Lift Works — Bascules, Counterweights and Chambers
chapters.intro: Before you cross, understand the machine under your feet. Each bascule is a steel leaf about 33 metres long, weighing, with its counterweight, over 1,000 tons. It pivots in a vast chamber inside the pier, open to view at certain points — and the whole lift, road gates to reopening, takes only a few minutes.

subchapters.title: Anatomy of a Bascule — Leaf, Trunnion and Counterweight
subchapters.text: Picture a seesaw sunk into the pier. The visible leaf — roadway and footways — reaches out over the river. At its root it is fixed to a pivot shaft, the trunnion, carried in bearings in the pier. Behind the pivot, inside the pier, hangs the counterweight end: a short, massively weighted tail containing about 422 tons of counterweight in lead and iron in the original design, so that leaf and tail nearly balance. Because the system is balanced, the engines overcome mainly friction and wind, not raw weight — which is why 1894 machinery could move it in a minute, and why a lift still looks so eerily effortless from the bank. When the leaf rises, the tail swings down into the bascule chamber, a cathedral-sized pit inside the pier.

subchapters.title: The Bascule Chambers — Cathedrals Under the Road
subchapters.text: The bascule chambers are among London's great hidden spaces: brick-vaulted pits beneath each approach, into which the counterweight tail descends as the bridge opens. They are not normally part of the standard visit — special tours run occasionally — but the exhibition's film and models show them, and from the walkway glass floor you can appreciate the geometry. The chambers must stay dry and maintained in a tidal river; their scale explains why the piers contain 70,000 tons of concrete. Think of the bridge as an iceberg: the photographed towers are perhaps a third of the structure; the rest is chamber, pier, machinery and anchorage, hidden below the waterline and the roadway.

subchapters.title: The Sequence of a Lift — Bells, Gates and a Minute of Rising
subchapters.text: A modern lift runs like a drill. At the appointed time, the team stops road traffic, closes the gates, checks the span is clear — the 1952 bus incident, coming later in this guide, is the cautionary tale drilled into the procedure — and signals the engine room. The bascules rise, typically to between 20 and 50 degrees for ordinary vessels, up to a maximum of 83 degrees for the tallest, taking about a minute. The vessel passes, the leaves lower, gates open, and traffic flows — the whole interruption often under five minutes. Around 800 lifts a year are performed, 24 hours a day, in all weathers, and each one is logged. If a lift happens during your visit, the faint hum and vibration you feel in the walkways is the machinery working directly beneath the towers.

subchapters.title: What Passes Through — Tall Ships, Warships and a Glorious Anachronism
subchapters.text: The traffic that justifies all this is gloriously varied: tall-masted sailing ships visiting the Pool, naval vessels calling at HMS Belfast's berth or proceeding upstream, barges, tourist boats with folding masts — and, several times a year, vessels that require the full 83 degrees. The bridge was designed for a working port of sailing ships; that the port moved downstream to Tilbury and beyond in the container era is why lifts fell from several thousand a year in the early decades — the bridge opened over 6,000 times in 1894's successors' busiest years by some reckonings — to today's roughly 800. Each modern lift is thus partly ceremony: the machine performing its original function for a river that has changed around it, by legal right, on 24 hours' notice.

chapters.caption: The bascules raised — each leaf balanced by over 400 tons of counterweight

chapters.title: The West Walkway — A Victorian Commuter Shortcut
chapters.intro: Step out 42 metres above the Thames. These walkways were not built as a tourist attraction: they were the pedestrian bypass, so foot traffic could cross over the top while the bascules were raised. Londoners mostly refused to climb, pickpockets moved in, and the walkways closed in 1910 for 72 years — which is why you get them now as a gallery in the sky.

subchapters.title: Why Walkways Exist — Crossing While the Bridge Is Open
subchapters.text: When the bascules rise, road traffic stops dead — but in 1894 a pedestrian detour to London Bridge was a serious cost to a working day. So the design carried foot passengers up the towers by lift or stair and across the high walkways, over the open span. The walkways were originally open-air, with the wind and weather of the river at 42 metres; the present glazing, added when they reopened as an exhibition in 1982, is the comfort you are enjoying. The concept was sound; the public was not persuaded. Most people preferred to wait a few minutes at street level rather than climb hundreds of steps — a verdict on Victorian pedestrian planning that every transport designer since has quietly understood.

subchapters.title: Closure in 1910 — Pickpockets and a Bad Reputation
subchapters.text: Empty, unpoliced and reachable only by long stairs, the walkways acquired a reputation as a haunt of pickpockets and prostitutes, and ordinary pedestrians avoided them — a death spiral of disuse. They were closed in 1910, after only 16 years, and stayed shut for over 70 years, becoming one of London's famous inaccessible spaces, visible to everyone and visited by no one except maintenance crews. During the Second World War the enclosed walkways served as a vantage for watching the river. Their reopening in 1982, as the centrepiece of the new Tower Bridge Exhibition, converted a failed transport idea into a successful museum — arguably the use they were always best suited for, since the view, not the shortcut, was the real product.

subchapters.title: Great Bridges of the World — The Walkway Exhibition
subchapters.text: Along the walkways you will find the exhibition of great bridges — large photographs and panels celebrating landmark crossings from the Golden Gate to the Millau Viaduct. It earns its place: Tower Bridge belongs to a family of heroic 19th- and 20th-century spans, and comparing them sharpens what is distinctive here — few great bridges are also machines, fewer still are machines that open in a capital city's centre, and none is dressed as a medieval castle. Note the company: the Forth Bridge shares this bridge's steel contractor, Arrol's of Glasgow; Brooklyn Bridge shares its hybrid suspension logic and its role as a city's emblem. You are standing inside one exhibit while reading about its peers.

subchapters.title: Open Windows and Photography
subchapters.text: Some walkway windows open — look for the designated photographic windows, where there is no glass between you and the shot. Photographers prize the upstream view toward the City at golden hour and the downstream sweep at dawn, but the honest secret is that this is one of the few London viewpoints that works in any weather: rain streaks the river silver, fog simplifies the skyline to silhouettes, and a lift below you reorganises every composition. The walkways face both ways — windows upstream and down — so work both sides before you cross. And look at the walkway structure itself between views: the lattice steelwork around you is original 1890s fabrication, painted and maintained, carrying the tie rods that hold this bridge together.

chapters.caption: The West Walkway, 42 metres above the Thames

chapters.title: The Glass Floor — Look Down, If You Dare
chapters.intro: Deep breath. In 2014 sections of the walkway floors were replaced with glass — 11 metres long in the West Walkway, each panel built from layers totalling 70 millimetres, weighing over 500 kilos, and rated to hold an elephant or two London taxis. Below you: buses, cyclists and the Thames, 42 metres straight down.

subchapters.title: Standing on Glass — What You Actually See
subchapters.text: Step out and look down, not ahead. Directly beneath the West Walkway glass runs the bridge deck: red buses, black cabs, cyclists and pedestrians streaming across, rendered toy-like by height, and on either side the Thames sliding past the piers. The vertigo most people feel lasts seconds, replaced by a strange privilege — you are watching the bridge work from inside its silhouette. If a lift begins while you stand here, you hold the best seat in London: the bascules rise beneath you, the gap widens, and a vessel slides through the middle of a road. Time your visit to a published lift time and aim to be on this glass for it; the bridge lift schedule is posted in advance precisely so visitors can do this.

subchapters.title: How the Panels Are Built — Five Layers and a Sacrificial Skin
subchapters.text: Each glass panel is a laminate of five layers, about 70 millimetres thick in total, designed so that even if a layer cracks the panel holds — the top layer is a sacrificial surface that can be replaced when scuffed by thousands of shoes. The panels, each weighing around 530 kilos, were winched into place during the 2014 installation, closing the walkways in phases. The steel frame around them is original walkway structure, adapted. Engineers rate the floor to hold the weight of an elephant or two black cabs — the standard reassuring comparison — and in practice it carries school groups lying flat for photographs, which is the real design load. A solid floor strip runs alongside the whole glass section, so nobody has to step onto it; crossing on the solid strip is a perfectly respectable choice.

subchapters.title: The Mirrored Ceiling and the Floating Photograph
subchapters.text: Look up in the West Walkway: a mirrored ceiling was installed above the glass floor so you can photograph yourself apparently floating over the river — lie on the glass, shoot upward, and the reflection gives you the down-view and your own figure in one frame. Silly? Absolutely. Worth it? Also absolutely, and the queue of adults waiting to do it proves the point. The mirror also has a subtler effect: it doubles the sense of height, reflecting the river into the ceiling, so even visitors who stay on the solid strip experience the drop. Exhibition design this playful, inside a Grade I listed machine, is a small lesson in how to make engineering legible to everyone who walks in.

subchapters.title: Heights, Nerves and Doing It Anyway
subchapters.text: A practical word for the nervous, from everyone who has crossed before you: the sensation peaks at the first step, when your eye measures the drop and your body briefly refuses to believe the glass. It fades fast — most people are sitting on it within a minute. Children have no problem at all and will try to educate their parents, loudly. If heights genuinely trouble you, the walkways still deliver: the window views are at the same level, the solid strip is generous, and the East Walkway's glass, added later, gives you a second chance on the return crossing with the downstream view. Nobody in the exhibition's history has been required to be brave; the bridge carries you either way, which was, after all, its original job description.
subchapters.directions: Continue across to the South Tower, then return along the East Walkway for the downstream view.

chapters.caption: The glass floor — road and river, 42 metres straight down

chapters.title: The Views — Reading London from Mid-River
chapters.intro: Use the walkways as what they really are: a free orientation lecture on London, delivered from the one viewpoint that stands in the river itself. Upstream is money, law and the old City; downstream is the working river that made the bridge necessary. Read both directions slowly before you descend.

subchapters.title: Upstream West — The Tower of London at Eye Level
subchapters.text: Face west, upstream. Closest on the north bank is the Tower of London — if you have just come from there, this is your victory lap: White Tower, curtain walls, green moat, all laid out like an architect's model, and the only public viewpoint from which you look slightly down on it. The fortress and the bridge frame each other; the Victorians clad the bridge in Gothic stone precisely so this pairing would look intentional. Beyond the Tower rises the City of London's cluster — the Walkie-Talkie, the Cheesegrater, the Gherkin and the rest of the nicknamed towers — and in the distance, still anchoring every panorama despite the competition, the dome of St Paul's Cathedral, which planning law protects in sightlines from viewpoints like this one.

subchapters.title: HMS Belfast and the Pool of London
subchapters.text: Moored mid-river below you is HMS Belfast, the Royal Navy town-class cruiser launched in 1938, which fired some of the opening shots on D-Day in 1944 supporting the Normandy landings, served in Korea, and is now a branch of the Imperial War Museum. Her berth is in the Pool of London — the stretch of river, from London Bridge to Limehouse, that was for centuries the legal quays of the world's greatest port, where ships queued tiers deep and the bascules of this bridge earned their keep letting them in and out. The Pool is quiet now — container ships dock far downstream — but Belfast, the Tower and this bridge preserve its outline like a labelled diagram.

subchapters.title: Downstream East — Wapping, Rotherhithe and Canary Wharf
subchapters.text: Turn around and look east from the East Walkway. The river bends away past the old wharves of Wapping on the north bank and Rotherhithe and Bermondsey on the south — warehouses now converted to flats, their hoists and signs often preserved — toward the towers of Canary Wharf, the docklands financial district built in the derelict docks from the 1980s. This was the working river: the greatest port in the world in this bridge's heyday, employing tens of thousands of dockers, lightermen and warehousemen. The geography explains the bridge's existence in one glance: everything east of here needed the river open; everything on both banks needed a road across. The bridge stands exactly on the seam between the two Londons, which is really the story of the whole city.

subchapters.title: The South Bank and the Shard
subchapters.text: Below the South Tower spreads the south bank: the Shard, at 310 metres western Europe's tallest building when it completed in 2012, rising behind London Bridge station; the old wharves of Bermondsey; and the Thames Path running west toward Borough Market, Shakespeare's Globe and the Tate Modern. From the walkway you can trace a full day's walking in one view — Tower, bridge, market, theatre, gallery — which is why this chapter doubles as itinerary advice. The south bank was historically the city's pleasure and industry margin — theatres outside the City's jurisdiction, tanneries, breweries, prisons — and its modern reinvention as a cultural promenade is written in the roofline below you: glass tower, converted warehouses, museum chimneys, all in a single sweep.

chapters.caption: Upstream from the walkway: the Tower, HMS Belfast, the City and the Shard

chapters.title: Stories in the Air — The Bus, the Biplane and the Jet
chapters.intro: No structure this public avoids incident, and Tower Bridge has collected three classics: a bus that jumped the gap in 1952, a biplane threaded through it in 1912, and a RAF jet flown under the walkways in 1968 as a protest. Each story is true, documented and better in the details than in the legend — here they are in full.

subchapters.title: Albert Gunter's Bus Jump — 30 December 1952
subchapters.text: On the night of 30 December 1952, Albert Gunter was driving the number 78 bus, Shoreditch to Dulwich, across the bridge when the bascule beneath him began to rise — a relief watchman had missed the warning-bell and gate sequence. The bus was near the edge of the south bascule, doing about 12 miles per hour. Gunter judged he could not stop, accelerated instead, cleared a gap of about three feet, and dropped some six feet onto the north bascule, which had not yet risen. Passengers were thrown about; remarkably, there were no serious injuries, though Gunter himself broke a leg in some accounts of the aftermath. The City Corporation gave him £10 and a day off, in honour of his quick thinking. The procedure for lifts was tightened, permanently — this is why modern lifts run like drills.

subchapters.title: Frank McClean Flies Through — August 1912
subchapters.text: On 10 August 1912 the pioneer aviator Francis — Frank — McClean flew his Short Brothers floatplane between the bascules and the high-level walkways of Tower Bridge, a gap he had no margin in, reportedly forced low by engine trouble and river traffic — accounts differ on how planned the stunt was. He became a celebrity overnight, then, unable to leave well enough alone, flew on under London Bridge, Blackfriars and Waterloo bridges. On the return run upriver, a gust caught the floatplane at Tower Bridge and put him in the Thames; he survived, the plane was recovered, and the photographs became classics of early aviation. McClean was no mere stuntman — he was a serious pioneer and astronomer who later served in the Royal Naval Air Service — but this flight, two years before the First World War, is what London remembers.

subchapters.title: The Hawker Hunter Incident — 5 April 1968
subchapters.text: On 5 April 1968, Flight Lieutenant Alan Pollock of the RAF, protesting the government's defence cuts and the failure to mark the RAF's 50th anniversary with a flypast, flew his Hawker Hunter jet unofficially over London landmarks — and through Tower Bridge, between the walkways and the roadway, at over 300 miles per hour. He was arrested on landing, charged, and discharged from the RAF on medical grounds without a court martial, amid considerable public sympathy. The flight remains one of the most famous unauthorised acts in RAF history. Standing on the walkway, look at the gap he used: at jet speed, with the river bends and the towers, the airmanship is as undeniable as the indiscipline. The bridge, characteristically, was undamaged and open for traffic throughout.

subchapters.title: Marilyn, the Marathon and Modern Moments
subchapters.text: The bridge keeps accumulating small histories. It starred in films and in the 2012 Olympic opening imagery, when its bascules rose for a speedboat carrying the Olympic flame — and a famous stunt double for the Queen's parachute sequence passed nearby in the same ceremony's film. The London Marathon crosses it at its halfway point, the one moment most runners remember. In 1977 it gained its red-white-and-blue paint; in 1997 a motorcade incident, when the bridge lifted in front of a US presidential entourage's route, reportedly caused diplomatic consternation and procedural reviews. None of this is in the official engineering record, and all of it is the bridge's real biography: a machine so central to London that the city's life keeps happening on it, whether scheduled or not.

chapters.caption: The bridge in London's life — lifts, marathons and the occasional jet

chapters.title: Down the South Tower — And Along the Blue Line
chapters.intro: Descend the South Tower — again, the stairs carry exhibition material the lift skips — and step outside onto the south bank. From here a blue line painted on the pavement, a small piece of exhibition design worth noticing, leads you under the southern approach to the final act: the Victorian Engine Rooms.

subchapters.title: The South Tower and Butler's Wharf
subchapters.text: The South Tower mirrors the North — steel frame, stone skin, exhibition levels — but its setting differs: you emerge into Southwark, among the converted warehouses of Butler's Wharf, built in the 1870s-80s as one of the largest tea and spice warehousing complexes on the river. The wharf buildings, with their overhead gangways for moving goods between warehouse and ship, fell derelict after the docks moved downstream and were regenerated in the 1980s-90s, with Terence Conran's design empire among the pioneers. The contrast is instructive and visible from the tower steps: on the north bank, a Norman fortress; on the south, Victorian warehouses; between them, a Victorian bridge — three centuries of Thames commerce in one eyeful, all now partly museums, none of them entirely so.

subchapters.title: The Blue Line — Wayfinding as Exhibition
subchapters.text: Follow the blue line. It is painted on the pavement from the South Tower, under the southern approach road, to the Engine Rooms entrance — a humble but effective piece of design that has guided millions of visitors through a junction where the exhibition otherwise loses people. It exists because the Engine Rooms are physically separated from the towers by the approach road, and visitors who rushed the towers used to miss them entirely. Do not miss them. The engine rooms contain the original machinery — the bridge's heart, preserved in situ — and for many engineers they are the best part of the visit. The walk takes two minutes; the line passes under the bridge's landward arches, where you can appreciate the masonry of the approaches, built by Webster's men to carry the road up to bridge level.

subchapters.title: St Katharine Docks — The Neighbour Across the Road
subchapters.text: Before you follow the blue line, look north across the road to St Katharine Docks, the enclosed dock basins immediately east of the Tower, opened in 1828 to Thomas Telford's engineering and now a marina of yachts and houseboats ringed by warehouses, pubs and flats. The docks and the bridge belong to the same story: a port pressing ever harder against the City's edge, demanding first basins, then a bridge that could open. The dock company's warehouses once handled ivory, spices, wine and marble; the ivory stores gave the basin its faintly exotic nickname in the trade. It is a two-minute detour and the calmest water in central London — a good place to let the towers' worth of information settle before the engine rooms.

subchapters.title: The Southern Approach and the Bridge's Landward Half
subchapters.text: Pause under the approach and consider the bridge whole. Its total length is 244 metres; the towers and opening span are only the centrepiece. The approaches — raised roadways on arches from both banks — carry traffic up to the level of the side suspension spans. Tolls were never charged to cross at street level, and crossing on foot has always been free; the bridge was a municipal gift, built by the City of London's Bridge House Estates, the ancient fund, dating to the 1200s, that maintains London's bridges from property income. Bridge House Estates still owns and maintains Tower Bridge today — the exhibition and the lifts are run by the same charitable fund that has looked after London Bridge for eight centuries, a continuity as remarkable as any machinery inside.

chapters.caption: The South Tower and the blue line to the Engine Rooms

chapters.title: The Victorian Engine Rooms I — Steam, Boilers and Accumulators
chapters.intro: For my money, the most underrated part of the visit: cavernous rooms under the southern approach holding the original 1894 machinery — steam pumping engines, coal-fired boilers and great hydraulic accumulators, painted green and red and polished like showpieces. This is the power station that the road on top was attached to.

subchapters.title: How Hydraulic Power Worked — Pressure Stored Like a Battery
subchapters.text: Understand the system in one idea: store energy in advance. The steam engines did not lift the bridge directly. They pumped water into accumulators — towering cylinders containing a piston loaded with massive weights — raising the weights and storing energy as water pressurised to about 750 pounds per square inch. When a ship approached, valves released that stored pressure to hydraulic engines at the bascules, which swung the leaves up in about a minute. Because the power was pre-stored, the bridge never waited for steam to build; the accumulators were, in effect, Victorian batteries, charged slowly and discharged fast. Six accumulators were installed across the bridge's engine rooms and tower bases, giving reserve enough for several lifts even if an engine stopped.

subchapters.title: The Steam Pumping Engines — 360 Horsepower in Green and Red
subchapters.text: The preserved pumping engines, built by Armstrong's of Newcastle, are compound steam engines of 360 horsepower each, driving pumps through great flywheels — engines you can walk around, under and between, at a scale modern plant rooms never allow. They ran, with their successors and a wartime spare, from 1894 until the system's retirement in the 1970s — over 80 years of continuous municipal service. Look at the finish: lagged cylinders, polished rods, maker's plates, oilers' cans still in place. Victorian engineers maintained machinery as a point of professional pride, and the engine-room crews — part of that staff of 80, working shifts around the clock — kept these engines in show condition while doing a dirty, hot, coal-fired job.

subchapters.title: The Boilers and the Coal — The Hidden Labour
subchapters.text: Behind the engines stood the boilers — originally Lancashire boilers, coal-fired by stokers working in heat and dust, raising steam day and night whether a lift was scheduled or not, because a port cannot wait for a boiler to warm. Coal arrived by barge and cart; ash left the same way. A third engine was installed in 1942, during the Second World War, as insurance against bomb damage to the originals — a 150-horsepower cross-compound engine by Vickers Armstrong with a nine-foot flywheel; it became redundant at modernisation and was donated to the Forncett Industrial Steam Museum in Norfolk, where it still runs on steam days. The two World Wars frame this room: coal, steam and vigilance, in a basement under a road, keeping London's river open.

subchapters.title: The Accumulators — Towers of Stored Energy
subchapters.text: Stand beside an accumulator and look up: a vertical cylinder from which rises a great loaded ram, the weight carried in a casing of iron and concrete — tons of mass held aloft by water pressure alone. As the pumps worked, the ram rose, storing energy; as the bridge lifted, it sank, delivering pressure at a steady rate no pump could match directly. The accumulator was the invention of William Armstrong, the Newcastle hydraulic pioneer whose firm supplied this machinery — the same principle powered hydraulic cranes, dock gates and lifts across Victorian Britain, and Tower Bridge is its most famous surviving showcase. The exhibition's cutaways and animations repay a minute's study: once you grasp the accumulator, every other machine in the room becomes a supporting character.

chapters.caption: The Victorian Engine Rooms — the original steam engines that lifted the bridge until 1976

chapters.title: The Victorian Engine Rooms II — Modernisation and the People Who Run It
chapters.intro: The steam system ran until the 1970s, when electric pumps and oil hydraulics replaced it — faster, cleaner and crew-light. The Victorian machinery was not scrapped but kept, lovingly, in place. This final engine-room chapter covers the changeover, the modern control system, and the small team that still lifts a listed monument 800 times a year.

subchapters.title: 1974–1976 — Electric and Oil Replace Steam and Water
subchapters.text: In 1974 the original operating system was largely replaced: electric motors driving oil-hydraulic pumps now power the bascules, controlled from a modern console — push-button lifts, in place of valve wheels and steam. The change cut the operating staff from dozens to a handful and ended the coal, the stokers and the round-the-clock steam watch. Crucially, the old machinery was preserved in situ as the exhibition's core, rather than sold for scrap — an early and enlightened act of industrial conservation, just as the walkways were being prepared for reopening. The new system was designed to be gentler on the 1894 structure, too: controlled acceleration and braking of a 1,000-ton leaf matters, and modern drives meter the forces in ways steam valves never could.

subchapters.title: The Modern Control Room — One Console, Total Oversight
subchapters.text: Displays show the modern control position: screens and cameras covering the span, the approaches and the river, interlocks that prevent a lift until gates are closed and the deck proven clear — the procedural ghost of Albert Gunter's bus — and communication with the Port of London Authority's river traffic service. A lift today is requested, scheduled, published online in advance, and executed by a small team with a checklist culture borrowed from railways and aviation. The bridge's website publishes lift times days ahead, which is how visitors time the glass floor — and how road users plan around the bridge. Transparency is part of the modern machine: in 1894 a lift was a surprise to everyone on the road; today it is a timetable.

subchapters.title: The Engine Rooms' Cats and Crews — A Staff of Eighty
subchapters.text: My favourite small detail from the tower displays belongs here in spirit: cats once lived in these engine rooms, officially, to keep rodents from the machinery and stores — every great monument has its unsung staff, and some of Tower Bridge's were cats. The human staff at the system's peak numbered about 80: engineers, stokers, lift operators, bridgemasters, toll-free gate staff, painters and labourers, many living in tied cottages and flats in the towers and approaches — there were once dwellings inside the bridge itself. The exhibition's oral-history material, drawn from retired staff and their families, recovers a whole workplace culture: night shifts during lifts for the night river traffic, fog duty, royal visits, and the pride of a crew whose work was on postcards worldwide and whose names were known to almost no one.

subchapters.title: Preservation in Working Order — Why It Matters
subchapters.text: The engine rooms are not a reconstruction: this is the actual plant, in its actual room, maintained by engineers who still understand steam. That authenticity is the exhibition's deepest claim. Industrial heritage usually survives as fragments — an engine in a museum hall, divorced from its building. Here, engine, accumulator, boiler house, bascule and river survive as one system, and you have walked the whole circuit in an hour: problem, design, towers, walkways, power. When school groups stand in this room, they are inside the machine, not looking at a picture of it. The Victorians built to last and maintained what they built; the best argument for preservation is simply that, 130 years on, so much of their work is still here to preserve.
subchapters.directions: Exit the Engine Rooms to the south bank pavement — west for the Shard and Borough Market, east back toward the Tower.

chapters.caption: Accumulators and engines — preserved in the rooms where they worked

chapters.title: Wrap-Up — Still a Working Bridge
chapters.intro: Here's the thought to take away: Tower Bridge is not a ruin, a replica or a museum piece that happens to look like a bridge. It is a working machine that has lifted for river traffic continuously since 1894, with river traffic still holding right of way over road traffic, by law. Most people only photograph it. You have been inside the machine.

subchapters.title: 800 Lifts a Year — River Still Rules the Road
subchapters.text: The bridge lifts around 800 times a year, 24 hours a day. Ships give 24 hours' notice, the team swings into action, gates close, and London's traffic simply waits, as it has since 1894. That legal priority — river over road — is a living fossil of the port city's constitution, preserved because Parliament wrote it into the bridge's founding Act and no one has ever dared repeal it. If you have flexibility left in your day, check the published lift times and watch one from the riverbank: the sight of a roadway rearing to 83 degrees, and a vessel gliding through the middle of a London street, never gets old, and from the bank you see the whole silhouette perform, which the walkway view, for all its drama, cannot give you.

subchapters.title: Crossing Back at Road Level — Free, As It Always Has Been
subchapters.text: Cross back north at road level to complete the experience — on foot, free, as it always has been. From the deck you feel the bridge's scale differently: the bascule joints under your feet, the chains of the side spans overhead, the towers rising sheer from the piers, and, if you pause at the centre — mind the traffic; use the pavements — the exact line where the two leaves meet, the seam of the seesaw. Look for the bridge's details at this level: the City arms, the lamp standards, the blue-and-white paintwork at close range. A bridge is a piece of street before it is a monument, and this street happens to cross the Thames on a machine.

subchapters.title: The Bridge at Dusk — Stay a Little Longer If You Can
subchapters.text: If you are here toward evening, stay. Tower Bridge is beautifully lit after dark — floodlighting that was renewed for the 2012 Olympics picks out the stone tracery and the blue steelwork — and the walk across at road level, with the Tower floodlit on the north bank and the river glittering on both sides, is one of the great free experiences in London. The south bank at dusk offers the classic photograph: bridge, river and City in one frame, with the walkways glowing. Photographers should try the riverbank by Butler's Wharf, east of the bridge, where the composition includes the full span without foreground clutter.

subchapters.title: Where Next — Two Banks, Two Days of London
subchapters.text: From here, both banks are yours. West along the south bank's Thames Path: the Shard, Borough Market, Shakespeare's Globe, Tate Modern and the Millennium Bridge to St Paul's — a single riverside walk through 400 years of London culture. East and north: back across for the Tower of London, St Katharine Docks with its marina in the old dock basins, and the City beyond. Or stay local: the pubs and restaurants of Butler's Wharf and Bermondsey Street, in the converted warehouses you saw from the walkway, are the neighbourhood the bridge built. Thanks for climbing up with me. The next time you see this bridge on a tea towel, you will know what the picture leaves out: piers, chambers, accumulators, cats — and a seesaw, dressed as a castle, still doing its day job.

chapters.caption: Tower Bridge at dusk — still a working bridge, lifting around 800 times a year

intro: Everyone photographs Tower Bridge; far fewer people go inside it. That's a shame, because the inside is where the story is: a Victorian steam-powered machine dressed up as a medieval castle, with walkways 42 metres above the Thames and a glass floor that lets you watch London traffic stream beneath your feet. The Exhibition takes you up the North Tower, across both high-level walkways, and down into the original Engine Rooms on the south bank. Allow about 75 minutes — and if you can, time your visit to a scheduled bridge lift, when the roadways rise for a passing ship. Let's climb.
mapNote: The Exhibition route is one-way and easy to follow. You enter at the North Tower (the Tower of London side), ride or climb to the top, and cross to the South Tower via the West Walkway (upstream views, glass floor). From the South Tower you can return along the East Walkway (downstream views) within the towers' exhibition level. Then you descend the South Tower, step outside, and follow the blue line painted on the pavement under the southern approach to the Victorian Engine Rooms — the final section. Exiting the Engine Rooms puts you on the south bank. Crossing the bridge at road level, on foot, is always free and separate from the Exhibition.
practical: One ticket covers everything: both towers, the walkways and glass floors, and the Victorian Engine Rooms. You don't need separate tickets for the Engine Rooms.
Check the bridge lift schedule before you visit (published on the Tower Bridge website) and time your entry so you're on the walkways during a lift — it's the highlight of the whole experience.
Allow 60–90 minutes. The Engine Rooms are a separate section on the south bank at the end, and visitors who rush the towers often skip them — don't.
The glass floor has a solid walkway alongside it the whole way, so anyone nervous about heights can cross comfortably and still enjoy the views.
Take the stairs in the North Tower if you can: the stairwell displays on the builders and divers are part of the exhibition. Lifts are available for step-free access.
Photography is allowed throughout, and some walkway windows open for glare-free shots — the best Tower of London photo in the city is from up here.
Crossing the bridge at street level is free; if you're short on time, even a walk across gives you the river views and the bascules up close.
subtitle: Inside London's most famous bridge — walkways, glass floor, and steam engines
title: Tower Bridge
